newsitem.title: UK: Governments urged to lead in healthcare rationing.
newsitem.headline: Governments urged to lead in healthcare rationing.

text.p: Governments, with the help of the medical profession, should take the lead in stimulating a public discussion about how to ration healthcare, a panel of health professionals told a British Medical Association conference on Friday.
"The problem is not whether or not we are going to ration, but how and who will take the lead," said David Eddy, advisor to the California-based Kaiser Permanente health maintenance organisation.

Eddy and other panellists said public apprehension about the rationing of healthcare was based on the misconception that it involved denying certain groups of people access to care, or entirely excluding certain procedures from health plans. He and other panellists said governments had an obligation to lead the debate and avoid misconceptions from taking hold.
Although representatives of Britain's Labour government were invited to attend the one-day conference, no-one agreed to do so, said Richard Smith, editor of the British Medical Journal.
"We are very unhappy no-one from government came," he told journalists.
Speaking about the practicalities of rationing, panellist Eddy said that if it is "done well, it will be done (at a level) of very fine clinical detail".

Citing evidence that screening for breast cancer is most effective for women over the age of 50, he said more deaths could be prevented if screening resources were concentrated on older women than spread across a broader population group. Eddy said he was expressing his own views and not those of Kaiser.
He said the longer governments and the profession waited to take decisions based on clinical evidence, the greater the risk that priorities will be set on an ad hoc basis.
Delegates to the conference overwhelmingly endorsed a resolution saying that "government has the obligation to take the lead in health care rationing."
Britain's Royal College of Physicians has already called for the creation of a national commission on healthcare priorities, according to Albert Weale of the University of Essex.
But panellists said they doubted Labour would endorse such a move.
Recent polls show that the British public recognises the need for rationing but also places a high value on the principle that citizens have their health needs met, Weale said.
"This is the tension in the debate," he added.
Weale recommended that a national poll on rationing that used techniques developed in focus group surveys be conducted to flush out public attitudes further.
"No matter how difficult it is, there is no excuse for not trying to understand public opinion before trying to change it," he said.
